story.label: The idea in five steps
story.disclaimer: Illustration of the idea, not results.

steps.text: A printed part isn't solid. The printer builds it from lines of melted plastic, and small gaps are left between the lines.
steps.alt: Drawing of a slice through a 3D-printed part. Rows of plastic lines sit on top of each other with small gaps between them, and the middle of the part is mostly hollow.

steps.text: The gaps can let liquid in. Disinfectant can soak into the part and stay there.
steps.cite: In one study, a third of the chemical treatments made printed PLA samples heavier, by up to 8.3% (Fleischer et al., 2020).
steps.alt: The same slice with droplets on the surface. Liquid runs down through the gaps between the plastic lines and collects inside the part.

steps.text: The idea: brush a thin coat of epoxy over the surface to close the gaps.
steps.alt: The same slice with a green layer of epoxy covering the top surface and filling the dips between the plastic lines.

steps.text: If the seal works, the liquid stays on the outside.
steps.alt: The sealed slice with droplets sitting on top of the green epoxy layer. No liquid is inside the part.

steps.text: But does the seal last after 20 rounds of disinfection?
steps.cite: That is what this project tests.
steps.alt: The sealed slice with droplets on top, a times-20 mark, a row of 20 small bars, and a question mark.

question.label: The question
question.text: What are the individual and combined effects of epoxy sealing and 20 cycles of 70% isopropyl alcohol disinfection on the liquid absorption, flexural strength, percent mass change, and dimensional stability of 3D-printed PLA?
plain: Does a thin coat of epoxy keep liquid out of a 3D-printed plastic part?
Does the part stay as strong, and keep its weight and size?
And is that still true after 20 rounds of cleaning with 70% isopropyl alcohol?

why.label: Why it matters
why.heading: Printing a tool is cheap. Cleaning it is the hard part.
